inspection.method: Direct inspection of the official GitHub repository README, Apache-2.0 license and latest release metadata, plus official OPA documentation for deployment, bundles, Rego, management APIs and decision logs.
gaps: This first-pass model explains architecture rather than benchmarking OPA latency, throughput or resource usage in a specific deployment topology.

content_map.problem: Policy decisions are easy to hardcode inside each service, which couples changing organizational rules to application releases and produces inconsistent policy logic across systems.
content_map.thesis: OPA separates policy decision-making from enforcement: applications provide structured context to OPA, OPA evaluates declarative Rego policy and data to return a decision, and the application remains responsible for enforcing that decision.
sections: Repository identity, release and integration entry points
How OPA works: rules, data, queries and decisions
Policy Decision Point versus Policy Enforcement Point
Rego as the declarative policy language
Decision logs, status and management APIs
concepts: distributed decision points with logically centralized management
mechanisms: An application reaches a point where it needs a policy decision and constructs structured input describing the request and context.
The application queries OPA rather than embedding the rule directly in application code.
OPA evaluates the input against loaded Rego policy and data and returns an allow/deny or richer structured decision.
The application acts as the enforcement point: it accepts, rejects or otherwise changes behavior based on the returned decision.
Bundles can update policy and data independently from the application code deployment lifecycle.
Decision Logs and Status APIs can report decision and runtime state to a management layer; this operational plane is separate from the decision itself.
examples: API authorization: service sends user, operation and resource context; OPA returns allow/deny; service enforces it.
Deployment placement: a platform can ask which clusters a workload is allowed to use instead of hardcoding placement rules in the platform service.

Agent governance experiment: an execution service can ask whether a specific actor/agent may perform a consequential operation before invoking the tool, while the execution service remains responsible for actually blocking or allowing the action.
claims: OPA is an open-source general-purpose policy engine and a graduated CNCF project.
OPA uses a high-level declarative language, Rego, for policies over structured data.
OPA is a policy decision point; integrated applications/services are policy enforcement points and must enforce returned decisions.
OPA can be integrated via REST, Go APIs/SDK and WebAssembly among other patterns.
Bundles allow policy and data to be distributed and reloaded independently of application deployment.
Decision Logs can contain policy query events and support masking sensitive fields before upload.
The latest GitHub release observed on 2026-08-26 was v1.19.1, published 2026-08-17.
evidence: Official repository README explains that services execute queries when policy decisions are needed and then enforce the returned decision.
Official OPA deployment documentation describes OPA as the PDP and applications as PEPs, and recommends placing OPA close to enforcement points when latency/availability matter.
Official Bundles documentation describes policy/data distribution and on-the-fly reload behavior.
Official Management APIs document Bundles, Decision Logs, Status and Discovery for distributed OPA deployments.
Official Decision Logs documentation describes logged decision events and data masking.
GitHub release metadata verifies v1.19.1 and its 2026-08-17 publication timestamp.
assumptions: A service that queries OPA is designed to treat OPA's answer as authoritative for the policy decision being delegated.
Policy inputs expose enough context for Rego to make the intended decision without moving the actual enforcement responsibility into OPA.
A production deployment chooses an OPA topology and policy-distribution mechanism appropriate to its latency, availability and freshness requirements.
limitations: OPA computes policy decisions; it does not force an application to obey them. The enforcement point remains part of the trusted computing boundary.

Separating policy from application code does not automatically produce a single central network service. OPA is commonly deployed close to enforcement points while policy management is logically centralized.
Bundle-based policy distribution is not the same as instantaneous global consistency; policy version and activation status matter during rollout.
Decision inputs and logs may contain sensitive context, so logging and masking must be designed deliberately.
A general-purpose policy engine does not decide which business rules are correct; policy modeling, ownership, tests and rollout governance remain organizational responsibilities.
open_questions: Which OPA deployment mode best fits a specific agent execution service: sidecar/local daemon, library/SDK or Wasm?
What policy bundle signing, versioning and rollout controls are required for high-consequence enterprise actions?
How should decision IDs and policy versions be connected to an execution ledger so a later audit can reconstruct both the action and the exact policy decision?

selection.requested_focus: How does OPA separate policy decision-making from enforcement, and what should I learn or try from that architecture?
coherent_core: OPA should be understood first as a decision engine, not as the component that performs or blocks the business action itself.
The application/PEP supplies structured context and remains responsible for enforcement; OPA/PDP evaluates Rego plus data and returns a decision.
This separation makes policy logic independently reviewable and changeable instead of scattering it through service code.
At scale, distributed OPA instances can stay close to enforcement while bundles and management APIs provide a separate policy-distribution and operational layer.
The smallest experiment should prove the separation by changing a Rego rule while leaving the calling application/request shape unchanged.
prerequisites: Difference between a policy decision and enforcement of that decision
Basic understanding of structured request/context data
Why independently versioned policy rules can be easier to review/test than hardcoded conditionals
drop_notes: Do not turn the explainer into a Rego language tutorial; syntax is secondary to the architectural separation.
Do not cover every OPA integration, Kubernetes admission pattern or ecosystem project in the first mental model.
Do not imply that OPA is a full authorization product/control plane; the project supplies a policy engine plus APIs and expects surrounding integration/management choices.
connections: Refines the existing policy-as-code concept with a concrete decision/enforcement boundary.
Reinforces controlled execution by showing one implementable authorization primitive around consequential work.
Creates a future connection between policy decision IDs/versions and execution-history evidence without claiming OPA itself is the execution ledger.

verification_candidates.question: What sensitive request data could appear in Decision Logs for the intended use case, and what masking rules are needed?
verification_candidates.reason: Official docs support masking, but the fields requiring protection depend on the application's policy input schema.
